statement: Three case reports from one US psychiatric hospital in a single year (Rainey and Crowder, 1975) describe young men, aged 18 and 19, who after street drugs sold as PCP, THC or methadone, and presumed by the authors to contain phencyclidine, had psychoses lasting 2 to 4 weeks: agitation, hostility, disorientation, unsteadiness, insensitivity to pain in one, hearing voices in two, and dangerous behaviour (one jumped from a third-floor window, landing uninjured; one kicked a window until its frame came loose); afterwards they remembered little or nothing of the illness, two of them nothing of the first two weeks. All three recovered within 2 to 4 weeks, one after he left the hospital on his own, and none showed psychosis at the last assessment reported (days to a month later), although one man's psychological tests at 13 days suggested a schizophrenic process with organic impairment that had improved a month later. The authors note that in earlier reports PCP's mind-altering effects usually lasted 18 to 24 hours and that only a few longer reactions were known. They could not say why their patients were ill for so long, and list possible reasons: the dose, slow breakdown of the drug, toxic breakdown products, individual sensitivity, or the drug setting off or worsening a schizophrenic process. No drug test confirmed PCP, the men's psychiatric histories are not given, and three case reports cannot show how often this happens or why. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: Doctors in 1975 described three young men who were in hospital for two to four weeks with a severe mental breakdown (psychosis) after street drugs they thought were PCP. They were confused, angry and heard voices, and one jumped from a high window. All three got better, and afterwards remembered little or nothing of their illness. Their drugs were never tested, and three cases cannot show how often this happens.
population: Three young men (aged 18 and 19) admitted to one psychiatric hospital in Detroit within a year
exposure: Street drugs sold as PCP, THC or methadone, presumed by the authors to contain phencyclidine; no toxicology (amounts, where known, are study conditions in the study card)
comparator: None; the authors compare with the usual duration of PCP effects reported in earlier studies
outcome: Duration and features of psychosis, recovery and memory of the episode
magnitude: Three cases; psychosis lasting 2 to 4 weeks (case 1 oriented without psychosis 14 days after the drug; case 2 improving from about 5 days after admission with amnesia for 2 weeks; case 3 psychotic until he left hospital on its 17th day); usual psychotomimetic effects 18 to 24 hours, as cited from earlier literature.

evidence.locator: Case Reports, Case 1 (p. 1076, both columns, to p. 1077, left column top)
evidence.extracted: A 19-year-old man, said by an anonymous caller to have taken PCP, was transferred 4 days later mute, staring, salivating and insensitive to pinprick; after seizure-like episodes he became assaultive and was secluded; 11 days after the drug he was more cooperative and 3 days later oriented with no psychotic signs, remembering nothing of the first 2 weeks.

evidence.locator: Case Reports, Case 2, 1st to 4th paragraphs (left column)
evidence.extracted: An 18-year-old man who took a drug sold as THC came to the emergency room after 30 more hours without sleep, hostile, suspicious, ataxic, disoriented and hearing chains; the day after admission he jumped from a third-floor window, landing uninjured; after 4 more days he became more aware and remembered nothing of the previous 2 weeks. Tests 13 days after the drug suggested a chronic schizophrenic process with residual organic impairment; a month later there was no psychosis and the impairment had improved. Three of his four friends were hospitalized and discharged within 2 to 3 days.

evidence.locator: Case Reports, Case 3 (left column, lower part, and right column)
evidence.extracted: A 19-year-old man arrested after refusing to answer questions in court was agitated, heard voices and believed he was poisoned; in hospital he was ataxic, walked around nude and thought he was still in jail; blood pressure rose from 110/64 to 160/115 on the 16th day; on the 17th day he left, improved greatly at home without medication, could not remember what had happened, said he had taken a pill sold as methadone, and a week later showed no psychosis.

evidence.locator: Discussion, 1st paragraph (p. 1077, right column) and continuation (p. 1078, left column)
evidence.extracted: The authors are reasonably certain the men took phencyclidine from their history of street drugs often found to contain it and from the clinical picture; no laboratory confirmation is reported. As cited from earlier literature, PCP's analgesia usually lasts 1 to 3 hours and its psychotomimetic effects 18 to 24 hours; prolonged reactions had been reported in 1 of 65 surgical patients (10 days) and in four people with chronic schizophrenia (more than 4 weeks). The authors do not know why their patients were ill for 2 to 4 weeks and list dose, slow metabolism, toxic metabolites, idiosyncrasy or precipitation or exacerbation of a schizophrenic process.

risk_of_bias.note: Three selected case reports with no toxicology and no psychiatric histories (editors' checklist high).

indirectness.note: Worded as a description of these cases.

publication_bias.note: Unusual cases are more likely to be published; reflected in the wording that no frequency can be given.

grade.reasoning: A descriptive claim resting on three case reports starts low and is downgraded two levels for risk of bias (no confirmed exposure, selected cases), giving very low. It establishes only that such courses were seen, not their frequency or cause.
